title: Salmon vs. sardines: omega-3, protein, and calories

seo.title: Salmon vs. sardines: omega-3, protein, calories
seo.meta_description: Salmon and sardines are both rich in protein and EPA+DHA. Salmon usually has more long-chain omega-3 per 100 g; bone-in sardines stand out for calcium.
seo.search_intent: Compare salmon and sardines for omega-3, protein, fat and calories using equal weights and clearly defined forms.

excerpt: Salmon and sardines are surprisingly close in protein and calories. Both provide EPA and DHA; cooked Atlantic salmon can land around 2 grams EPA+DHA per 100 grams, while canned sardines are often around 1.4 grams, depending on species and product.
content_html:
A salmon fillet and a can of sardines look like very different foods, but the gap narrows once they are compared in equal amounts. Both provide substantial protein and meaningful EPA and DHA; salmon usually comes out ahead for long-chain omega-3, while bone-in sardines bring something a boneless fillet cannot match: far more calcium.

What actually changes in a 100 g comparison

Form matters. The table below compares cooked Atlantic salmon with drained canned sardines. A specific can can differ because of packing liquid, added salt, species, and how thoroughly it is drained.

NutrientCooked Atlantic salmonCanned sardines, drained
Calories~180–210~185–210
Protein~20–23 g~24–25 g
Fat~10–13 g~10–12 g
EPA+DHA~1.8–2.2 g~1.3–1.5 g

The first useful result is how much the calorie ranges overlap. There is no automatic split between “high-calorie salmon” and “lighter sardines”: both can land around 190–210 calories per 100 g. Oil retained by sardines after draining can move the number upward, while salmon species and fat content also matter.

Protein usually tilts slightly toward drained sardines. If sardines provide about 24–25 g/100 g and cooked salmon about 20–23 g/100 g, a 4-ounce serving works out to roughly 27–28 g protein from sardines versus about 23–26 g from salmon. That is a real difference, but either fish easily serves as the main protein source in a meal.

Omega-3 creates a wider gap than protein

NIH lists 1.83 g EPA+DHA in 3 ounces of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon and 1.19 g in 3 ounces of drained canned sardines in tomato sauce. Converted to 100 g, that is about 2.15 g versus 1.40 g. In that example salmon supplies roughly 0.75 g more EPA+DHA per 100 g, or about 54% more.

That does not make sardines a minor omega-3 source. More than 1 g EPA+DHA per 100 g is still a substantial amount. Neither fish has one fixed value, either: species, origin, feed, and the exact canned product can all shift the result, so the numbers are best read as a useful scale rather than a universal constant.

With sardines, edible bones and salt change the picture

The largest nutritional difference is calcium when the softened bones are eaten. A USDA reference for canned bone-in sardines is around 380 mg calcium per 100 g, while cooked boneless Atlantic salmon is roughly 10–15 mg/100 g. The advantage does not come from unusually calcium-rich sardine flesh; much of it comes from eating the mineralized skeleton.

The practical trade-off with a canned product is often sodium. As a reference point, canned sardines can be around 300 mg sodium/100 g, compared with roughly 60 mg/100 g in cooked salmon with no salt added. Labels matter here because added salt, sauce, and reduced-sodium products can move canned sardines well away from that example.

So which one makes more sense?

If your main goal is maximizing EPA and DHA for the same weight of fish, Atlantic salmon usually has the edge. If you want a compact food that combines protein, marine omega-3, and a large calcium contribution, bone-in sardines have an unusually strong profile. Calories do not produce a fixed winner: the ranges are close enough that packing oil and the specific product can matter more than the fish name.

There is little nutritional reason to treat this as an either-or choice. Salmon and sardines cover the same core strengths with different extras: salmon tends to lead on EPA+DHA, while sardines stand out for calcium and shelf-stable convenience. If sodium or calories are priorities, the label and preparation are more useful than a generic comparison.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3, salmon or sardines?
faq.answer: In NIH examples, cooked Atlantic salmon is about 2.15 g EPA+DHA per 100 g versus roughly 1.40 g for drained canned sardines in tomato sauce.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Canned sardines often provide about 24–25 g/100 g versus roughly 20–23 g in cooked salmon.

faq.question: Why are canned sardines high in calcium?
faq.answer: Their softened bones are usually edible. A USDA reference is around 380 mg calcium/100 g for bone-in canned sardines versus roughly 10–15 mg/100 g in cooked boneless salmon.
